techniques.name: Inclusion-Exclusion
techniques.description: To count objects with **none** of a set of properties, alternately add and subtract counts of objects having at least each combination of properties. For properties $A_1, \ldots, A_n$, the count of objects with none of them is $\sum_{T \subseteq [n]} (-1)^{|T|} f_{\geq}(T)$, where $f_{\geq}(T)$ counts objects having at least the properties in $T$.
techniques.when_to_use: When you can compute $f_{\geq}(T)$ easily for every $T$ (often it factors into a product), but computing the exact count $f_{=}(\emptyset)$ directly is hard.

techniques.name: Double Counting / Switching the Order of Summation
techniques.description: Count the same set $S$ of pairs (or triples) in two different orders. If $S = \{(a, b) : a \in A,\, b \in B(a)\}$, summing first over $a$ gives $\sum_a |B(a)|$; summing first over $b$ gives $\sum_b |A(b)|$. Equating the two sums yields an identity.
techniques.when_to_use: Whenever you need to relate two sums involving binomial coefficients or other combinatorial quantities. The key step is always identifying the correct set of pairs to double-count.

techniques.name: Inner Sum Collapse via Substitution
techniques.description: After an inclusion-exclusion, swap the order of summation so the inner sum runs over the 'excess' properties. The inner sum often evaluates to zero unless the outer index equals a specific value, collapsing the double sum. The identity $\sum_{k=j}^{n} (-1)^{k-j} \binom{k}{j} = [j=n]$ is a typical example.
techniques.when_to_use: When the I-E formula produces a double sum $\sum_T \sum_{\text{objects}} (-1)^{|T|}$. Interchange summation, identify the inner sum as an alternating binomial sum, and collapse.

techniques.name: Generating Functions
techniques.description: Encode a sequence $a_0, a_1, a_2, \ldots$ as $A(x) = \sum_n a_n x^n$ (ordinary) or $\hat{A}(x) = \sum_n a_n x^n / n!$ (exponential). Algebraic identities on $A(x)$ correspond to combinatorial identities on the $a_n$.
techniques.when_to_use: Recurrences, convolutions, asymptotic estimates. The EGF is natural when objects have labeled components (permutations, set partitions). The OGF is natural for unlabeled objects.

techniques.name: q-Analogues
techniques.description: Replace ordinary integers and factorials with their $q$-counterparts: $[n]_q = 1 + q + \cdots + q^{n-1}$, $[n]_q! = [1]_q [2]_q \cdots [n]_q$, and the $q$-binomial coefficient $\binom{n}{k}_q = [n]_q! / ([k]_q! [n-k]_q!)$. The $q$-binomial counts $k$-dimensional subspaces of $\mathbb{F}_q^n$ and also equals $\sum_{w} q^{\text{inv}(w)}$ over permutations with descent content $(k, n-k)$.
techniques.when_to_use: When ordinary counting formulas have natural 'stat' refinements (inv, maj, etc.) or when counting over finite fields $\mathbb{F}_q$.

techniques.name: Rook Polynomials
techniques.description: For a board $B \subseteq [n] \times [n]$, the rook numbers $r_k(B)$ count ways to place $k$ non-attacking rooks on $B$. The rook polynomial $R_B(x) = \sum_k r_k x^k$ encodes these. The hit numbers $N_j$ (full non-attacking placements with exactly $j$ rooks on $B$) are recovered from the $r_k$ via $N_n(x) = \sum_k r_k (n-k)! (x-1)^k$.
techniques.when_to_use: Permutation problems with position restrictions. The derangement formula is the $B = $ diagonal case; ménage is $B = $ diagonal plus super-diagonal (mod $n$).

techniques.name: Determinants from Factored Sums
techniques.description: When an inclusion-exclusion sum $\sum_{T} (-1)^{|T|} f_{\leq}(T)$ has $f_{\leq}(T)$ factoring as a product over pairs $(i,j)$, the Leibniz formula for the determinant exactly captures the alternating sum. The result is a determinant of the matrix $[g(i,j)]$.
techniques.when_to_use: I-E over ordered sets (e.g., descent sets, paths) where the 'at-least' function $f_{\leq}$ factors as a product. If $f_{\leq}(s_1, \ldots, s_k) = \prod_i h(s_i, s_{i+1})$, the I-E sum becomes a determinant.

techniques.name: Möbius Inversion on the Boolean Lattice
techniques.description: The inclusion-exclusion formula $f_{=}(S) = \sum_{T \supseteq S} (-1)^{|T|-|S|} f_{\geq}(T)$ is exactly Möbius inversion on the Boolean lattice $2^{[n]}$, where the Möbius function is $\mu(S,T) = (-1)^{|T|-|S|}$.
techniques.when_to_use: Any time you recognize I-E as a special case of Möbius inversion. Generalizes to arbitrary posets in §3.

techniques.name: Bijective Proof
techniques.description: Prove $|A| = |B|$ by constructing an explicit bijection $\varphi: A \to B$. The bijection must be clearly defined, injective, and surjective. Often the inverse is the more natural map to define.
techniques.when_to_use: When two combinatorial quantities are equal and there is a natural correspondence between the objects. Also useful for proving recurrences (e.g., $D(n) = (n-1)(D(n-1)+D(n-2))$).

techniques.name: Finite Differences
techniques.description: The forward difference operator $\Delta$ acts by $(\Delta f)(k) = f(k+1) - f(k)$. Then $\Delta^m f(0) = \sum_{j=0}^m (-1)^{m-j} \binom{m}{j} f(j)$. If $f(k) = b(k)$ counts objects with 'at least $k$ properties' in a symmetric I-E setup, then $a(m) = \Delta^m b(0)$ counts objects with 'exactly $m$ properties.'
techniques.when_to_use: Symmetric I-E (when $f_{\geq}(T)$ depends only on $|T|$). The formula $a(m) = \Delta^m b(0)$ is cleaner than writing out the full alternating sum.
